newsitem.title: USA: Pressure mounts on Columbia as CalPERS eyes lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Columbia as CalPERS eyes lawsuits.

text.p: Embattled Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. came under more pressure Tuesday when the largest U.S. public pension fund said it was evaluating its position on the company in light of lawsuits brought by three other state pension funds.
The California Public Employees' Retirement System, or CalPERS, said it will examine lawsuits filed against Columbia officials by the state pension funds of New York, Florida and Louisiana.

"We have about 3.7 million shares (in Columbia). We're evaluating our position right now. We have no plans at this point, but we'd like to take a look at some of these other lawsuits," a spokesman for CalPERS told Reuters.

CalPERS' scrutiny of Columbia may broaden the legal challenges being brought against the Nashville, Tenn.-based hospital giant, even as a massive federal probe continues to rock the company and depress its stock price.

The federal investigation led Tuesday to the arraignment in Fort Myers, Fla., of three mid-level company executives on charges of Medicare fraud, to which all three pleaded innocent. They were Robert Whiteside, director of reimbursements at Columbia headquarters; Michael Neeb, chief financial officer in the northern Florida division; and Jay Jarrell, chief executive in the southwest Florida region. Each is charged with conspiracy and fraud and, if convicted, faces up to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $1.25 million.

In a statement released Tuesday, Columbia senior vice president Victor Campbell said, "We are confident that any individuals accused of possible wrongdoing will be presumed innocent, afforded due process and provided their day in court. On our part, we will work with all the appropriate agencies, and are continuing with our own internal investigation."

Reflecting a house-cleaning under new chief executive officer Dr. Thomas Frist, Columbia said Tuesday that three more top executives have resigned. Samuel Greco, senior vice president for financial operations; Stephen Braun, general counsel; and Jamie Hopping, western group president, have quit or said they will soon do so, a company spokesman said.

Chief financial officer Robert Stearns resigned earlier this month, following by two weeks the ouster by the board of directors of former company chief executive Richard Scott and president David Vandewater.
Discussions between federal investigators and company attorneys continued Tuesday, the spokesman said.

The company declined to comment on a report that Healthsouth Corp. was interested in buying all or parts of Columbia, such as its rehabilitation facilities, surgery centers, occupational clinics and diagnostic units.
The only business that Columbia has put on the block is its home healthcare unit, the spokesman said.
Healthsouth, a Birmingham, Ala.-based owner of rehabilitation hospitals and other medical service centers, could not immediately be reached for comment.

A spokesman for the New York State Comptroller's office said it has been named lead plaintiff in a consolidated legal action against Columbia officials that includes the state pension funds of Florida and Louisiana.
The state pension funds, which are Columbia shareholders, have alleged that Columbia's officers and directors put the value of the company's stock at risk.
Shares in Columbia fell 62.5 cents to $33 on the New York Stock Exchange. Since the federal probe surfaced in March, Columbia's stock value has declined by about a third.

The company has more than 600 million common shares outstanding. With 342 acute-care hospitals and dozens of other locations, Columbia is the largest for-profit hospital company in the United States. It is also one of the nation's largest employers with 285,000 employees.
